tagline: From cotton country to marshes, the Mississippi shapes work and travel.
intro: This Louisiana river journey links agricultural country with the marshes of the Mississippi Delta. Tallulah lies seven miles southwest of the Mississippi itself; farther south, Port Allen’s riverfront looks across the water toward Baton Rouge. At Venice, Highway 23 reaches the last community along the river accessible by automobile.

One documented chapter of road building came in 1966, when 2.6 miles between Blackhawk and Shaw were resurfaced as part of the Mississippi River Parkway, or Great River Road, project. Flood protection was changing too: in the 1980s, the Fifth Louisiana Levee Board and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers worked on enlarging the Acme–Blackhawk levee.

Begin the southward sequence at Gassoway on US 65, then Tallulah and the agricultural village of Waterproof. Beyond Blackhawk, the town stops lead through New Roads, Port Allen and Donaldsonville, then toward Gretna across from New Orleans. The journey ends at Venice, a base for fishing and offshore oil and gas services.

moments.title: Waterproof
moments.text: Waterproof’s name describes relative safety from flooding before the Mississippi levee system was built. It was never a guarantee: the village was among the places affected when floodwaters from the Ferriday crevasse inundated the region in 1922. Agriculture remains central to this Tensas Parish village, where cotton is the main commodity crop and corn and soybeans also matter. Mechanization has reduced the demand for farm labor.

moments.title: Donaldsonville
moments.text: Donaldsonville elected Pierre Caliste Landry mayor in 1868, making him the first African American elected to that office in the United States. He had been enslaved and educated on a plantation owned by the Bringier family. After the war he became an attorney, served in both houses of the state legislature and became a Methodist Episcopal minister. The city’s Black community grew after the war as freed people joined those who had sought safety near Union forces. The River Road African American Museum is located here. Since 2008, the museum has been included on the Louisiana African American Heritage Trail.

moments.title: Venice
moments.text: The road journey reaches a working maritime community at Venice, the southern terminus of the Great River Road. Louisiana Highway 23 provides automobile access to this last community along the Mississippi, surrounded by marshes and wetlands. Offshore oil and gas discoveries in the twentieth century brought economic growth and established Venice as a service point for Gulf petroleum platforms. Commercial fishing and sport fishing share the local economy with services for offshore oil and gas. Anglers depart for Port Eads near the river’s mouth, while the port’s offshore work includes logistics, fueling and transport for drilling rigs and production platforms.
